w: Restored 16th-century half-timbered house on Henley Street where William Shakespeare was born in 1564 and spent his childhood. Grade I listed since 25 October 1951, it is now a small museum run by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust, drawing visitors into the rooms where England's most famous playwright grew up.
s: Half-timbered house where Shakespeare was born, 1564
_facts: 16th-century half-timbered house on Henley Street
Believed birthplace of William Shakespeare, 1564
Grade I listed since 25 October 1951
Run as a museum by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust

w: Built onto the side of the Royal Shakespeare Theatre on the site of the Victorian Shakespeare Memorial Theatre, destroyed by fire in 1926. Designed by Michael Reardon with a deep thrust stage seating around 450, it opened in 1986 with The Two Noble Kinsmen, and the Queen attended its official opening that November.
s: Thrust-stage RSC theatre opened by the Queen in 1986
_facts: Built onto the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, opened 1986
Deep thrust stage seating around 450
Opening production: The Two Noble Kinsmen, directed by Barry Kyle
Queen Elizabeth II opened it on 13 November 1986

w: Grade I-listed house owned by William Shakespeare's daughter Susanna and her husband Dr John Hall, who married in 1607. It holds a collection of 16th- and 17th-century paintings and furniture, an exhibition on Hall's medical practice, and a walled garden of plants he may have used in treatments before the couple moved to New Place.
s: Shakespeare's daughter and her doctor husband's house
_facts: Owned by Susanna Hall (Shakespeare's daughter) and Dr John Hall, married 1607
Grade I listed
Exhibition on John Hall's medical practice
Walled garden of period medicinal plants

w: Late medieval masonry bridge with 14 pointed arches spanning the River Avon at the ford that gave Stratford its name. Built around 1484 and funded by Hugh Clopton, later Lord Mayor of London, it replaced a timber crossing first recorded in 1235; an arch was destroyed in 1642 to block Cromwell's army, and it still carries the A3400 today.
s: 1484 stone bridge still carrying traffic over the Avon
_facts: Built c.1484, funded by Hugh Clopton, future Lord Mayor of London
14 pointed stone arches, replacing a timber bridge recorded from 1235
An arch was destroyed in 1642 to block Cromwell's army
Grade I listed and a scheduled monument

w: Chapel Street house standing next door to the ruins and gardens of New Place, the site of William Shakespeare's final residence in Stratford. New Place itself is gone, but Nash's House survives alongside its garden remains, marking the spot where the playwright's own house once stood in the heart of town.
s: House by the ruins of Shakespeare's own final home
_facts: On Chapel Street, Stratford-upon-Avon
Stands next to the ruins and gardens of New Place
New Place was Shakespeare's final residence

w: Farmhouse tied to Mary Arden, mother of William Shakespeare, in the village of Wilmcote three miles from Stratford. Confusion over which building Mary actually lived in led a nearby farm to be preserved in the 20th century under her name, though it was later renamed Palmer's Farm; both houses are Grade I listed and open to visitors.
s: Farmhouse tied to Shakespeare's mother, Mary Arden
_facts: Wilmcote, about three miles from Stratford-upon-Avon
Named for Mary Arden, mother of William Shakespeare
The historically correct house was later identified as Palmer's Farm
Both farmhouses are Grade I listed
